result: The authors hypothesized and demonstrated that stimulus-driven local increases in alpha power result from a mixture of two effects: a reduction in alpha oscillatory power and a simultaneous increase in broadband power. After correcting for broadband baseline shifts, alpha oscillations consistently decrease in response to visual stimulation within the receptive field.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirmed this central finding. Reviewer 1 stated the results present 'compelling evidence' for spatial specificity and praised the 'careful approach to isolating and dissociating overlapping, but distinct, activities in the frequency domain.' Reviewer 2 found the 'model-based approach for separating alpha from broadband power changes is especially convincing and well-motivated.' The editor described the evidence as 'important and convincing.'

result: Alpha pRFs have similar center locations to broadband pRFs but are 2-4 times larger, with pRF size systematically increasing with eccentricity for both alpha and broadband. The slopes of size vs. eccentricity functions are about three times larger for alpha than for broadband.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 raised significant concerns about this finding, stating 'as broadband pRF models were on average better fit to the data than alpha pRF models...I wonder if this could entirely explain the larger Alpha pRF (i.e. worse fits lead to larger pRFs). There was no analysis to rule out this possibility.' Reviewer 3 also noted 'there wasn't any formal statistical test to back up any of the claims (not a single p-value is mentioned).' While reviewers 1 and 2 did not challenge these findings, the lack of statistical testing and potential confound with model fit quality leaves this result uncertain.

result: For visually selective electrodes in V1-V3, the alpha pRF model explains 37% of cross-validated variance, while non-visually selective electrodes show close to 0% variance explained. In dorsolateral maps, alpha pRF models explained about 24% of variance in visually responsive electrodes.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 raised critical concerns about sample size and statistical independence: 'The crucial results of Figure 4,5 hang on 53 electrodes from four patients...Almost half of these electrodes (25/53) are from a single subject. Data and statistical analysis seem to just pool all electrodes, as if these were statistically independent, and without taking into account subject-specific variability.' Reviewer 3 emphasized 'it is impossible to know if the results could be skewed by a single unrepresentative patient' and that 'N of subjects should also be explicitly specified next to each result.'

result: Low-frequency broadband (3-26 Hz) pRFs had positive gain and small size similar to high-frequency broadband (70-180 Hz), unlike alpha pRFs which had negative gain and large size. The stimulus-related broadband elevation extends down to 3 Hz or lower in V1-V3, but only to about 25 Hz in dorsolateral cortex.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted this finding without criticism, and it addresses the important methodological question of whether low-frequency broadband could confound alpha measurements. The reviewers accepted the authors' approach to dissociating broadband from oscillatory components, with Reviewer 2 stating the 'model-based approach for separating alpha from broadband power changes is especially convincing.'

result: Baseline correction for broadband shifts dramatically improved alpha pRF modeling: cross-validated variance explained was about 4 times higher (43% vs 10% median), pRF gain became consistently negative (29/31 electrodes) rather than mixed, and pRF size showed the expected increase with eccentricity.
evaluation: All reviewers praised this methodological approach. Reviewer 1 stated 'the authors employ contemporary methods for dissociating unique changes in alpha power from superimposed and concomitant broadband frequency range changes. This is an important confound in estimating changes in alpha power not employed in prior studies.' Reviewer 2 called it 'especially convincing and well-motivated.' The editor noted this work 'advocates that stimulus-driven alpha suppression is precisely tuned.'

result: Alpha coherence between electrodes is higher than broadband coherence, especially between neighboring electrodes, with alpha coherence declining from about 0.6 between neighbors to baseline (~0.35) by about 1 cm. The highest coherence occurs at the peak alpha frequency.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these coherence findings. Reviewer 1 noted the work provides 'strong supportive findings' overall, and the coherence data support the interpretation that alpha oscillations are spatially synchronized, consistent with the larger pRF sizes observed.

result: ERP regression had minimal effects on broadband and alpha response amplitudes, pRF locations, and cross-validated variance explained in pRF models (except for a handful of electrodes in dorsolateral maps).
evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted 'the authors employ many important controls in their processing of data,' implicitly accepting this methodological validation. No reviewer challenged the ERP regression approach or its minimal impact on results.

result: The large size and negative valence of alpha pRFs can explain key features of exogenous visual attention, with spatial profiles of attention and alpha pRFs showing three parallels: spatial spread increases with eccentricity, asymmetry spreading further into periphery, and center/surround organization. The timing matches as exogenous attention peaks at ~100ms (one alpha cycle).
evaluation: The editor specifically highlighted this contribution, stating the work demonstrates alpha's 'potential role in exogenous cuing attention.' Reviewer 2 called 'the link to exogenous attention behavioral findings (figure 8)...very interesting.' Reviewer 1 noted this represents 'some advance of prior work,' though the interpretation is somewhat speculative.

result: The broadband pRF is largely contained within the alpha pRF (92.3% overlap in V1-V3, 98.0% in dorsolateral), which is significantly greater than shuffled controls (30.0% and 25.7% respectively).
evaluation: While this quantification was not directly challenged, Reviewer 3's concerns about the V1-V3 vs. dorsolateral electrode assignment apply here: 'Out of 53 electrodes, 27 were doubly assigned as both V1-V3 and dorsolateral...This double assignment didn't make sense to me and I wasn't convinced by the authors' reasoning. I think it needlessly inflates the N for comparing the two groups and casts doubts on the robustness of these analyses.'

result: Prior studies (Klink et al. 2021, Takaura et al. 2016, Harvey et al. 2013, Luo et al. 2024) reported alpha power increases when stimuli were in receptive fields, contrasting with the traditional view of alpha suppression.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly noted 'There are important findings in the literature preceding the author's work that are not sufficiently highlighted or cited,' specifically mentioning 'prior work has examined the impact of using different frequency ranges to estimate RF properties, for example ECoG studies in the macaque by Takura et al. NeuroImage (2016)...as well as prior ECoG work by the author's team of collaborators (Harvey et al., NeuroImage (2013)).' This indicates the reviewers accepted these prior findings as established context.
